He was born in... I was born in 1888. He was born in 1889. Remember the date of his birthday? On the... On the 15th of June. And I was born on February 2nd, 1889. 1888. 1888. And we were ready to start with madeleine. And after he put out madeleine, he asked my dad and my mother to get them a violin. So he started learning violin from Mr. Baboy, an old cripple fellow. And he learned him how to play violin. And after he started playing violin, he got so that he started playing with Mr. Teton. They called him Teton, but his name is Adolf Alexander. And he was playing violin under Teton. As I was saying, his name is Adolf Alexander.
We know the young Alexander.

Well, he's his father. He lives on Dernan, New Orleans. And then my brother came to my father and mother and told him that he said he had a man playing. Yes, I knew him. He was a travel player.

He was a travel player. Yes. And, but nevertheless, he used to, after he quit the job, well, I'd taken his job on Rylan and Beaville at Mr. Michel. It's a juror store. That's his first job with cornet out there. After he left Bally, he said that he told my mother and father that he could not be heard and he wanted to get a cornet. So he takes my dad and my mother, brought him a cornet and he started fooling around with him. And then our dog Alexander, he used to take and play cornet while he showed him. And he used to play with Valtou, old violin player. He was playing violin at that time. And what happened when he started playing? The first job it was at the Lake Lucian Pavilion. That's the first job he played on cornet. Well, they've taken liking to him. So ever since that, he started fooling with cornet and playing cornet with the band.
He gave up the violin. He gave up the violin. When did he play on the mandolin? He said he was the first.

Then he played on the mandolin a little bit, but he wasn't playing with no band with the mandolin. But he could play. And he also was playing card then. I guess you know something about the card, Mr. Roussel. Sure. That card with that pull out and push in. The squeeze box. And then Manuel Manetta still is the first.
Manuel Manetta, that is his best friend.

And that is, he's from over the river. Yes. We know him. He is to play with Freddie. He is to play a violin with Freddie. And so you see, after he started playing the card then, well, he picked the line to it, but he dropped it all. And I had the cornet. He had it here, but I didn't, it then got so old, so I had to do way with it. Because it's the same as my sister, his family. She told it over to me about three weeks ago. Oh, yeah.

Well, I got his little cornet now. You don't have it now? No. He went to Chicago with the cornet and then he bought a new cornet. And this fellow here, just remember what he was for, he's dead now. But he's lived.
Well, then, then, Herb Moran maybe had it right?

Well, Moran is the one, excuse me, Moran is the one that bought his cornet. Because when he came down here before he died, he told me that Fred is cornet, when Fred died, he bought it from Sadie or his wife up there. And he's been having it and playing down here with it. And he showed it to me. Of course, nevertheless, I was fooling cornet myself a little bit because Mal Perez would give me ideas and he'd give me a lesson. You'd have to beat the value of the time before you pick up an instrument.
Learn to soft edge and all that.

That's the time you had to pick. You couldn't have no instrument. You had to take and use your feet to hold that time and take and get the value of the time before you get an instrument. Just like you say, one, two, three, four. One, two, three. Wash time, six, eight. Anything but the value of the music. That's what they wanted. Now, after when the same time come, Mr. Broussard, I left the job about a couple years after that. About two years from the place that I had taken from him. Then I picked up all the guitars as well as Bud Scott.
He was sure of me.
He's a great guitarist and a violin too. He's good. Now he went away. Of course, I couldn't say if he's living up there.
He died several years ago.

He was a great guitarist and a violinist. He's the one that composed that, the Wildcat, the Bumperche. What was that? Everything. He's the one that composed that. Now, we see, well, I used to play at the Economy Hall around the corner. And after that, I played at the Copperhead Hall. That was when I started playing. I had the Magnolia Band. Who was in that? Well, they had a fellow by the name of Dave Dupas. He used to play clarinet. And they had a fellow by Maurice Durand who was playing cornet. A new, uh... And after that, the band was just coming up. And we had this here fellow, Arnold... Arnold... Arnold... Uh... What's his name? Arnold Dupas. He was playing drum. His brother was playing clarinet. He was playing drum.
Baby Doss talking about Arnold Dupas.

And then they had... We had another fellow by the name of Sidney Desvien. He used to play clarinet too. Also, he used to work around for the band. And then he was playing on the part of the street. Well, I wasn't there. That's what they called the Magnolia Band at that time. And after that, we got to be... We broke it up and we put the Cherry Blossom Band. We broke up that and then I started getting... There's another man. And after we started getting that Cherry Blossom Band, then we continued. Then we bust up again. Then we started getting the band better and better. And I went up on third and... And magazine where Joe Oliver was working as a butler. He was a butler. He used to be a butler in that house. Doing garden work. And I went to him and seen him and talked to him about making him a band. And he wasn't playing with nobody. And he wasn't so extra. He wasn't so built up for reputation.
That's what I heard. He just started pretty late. He was not.

He was no reputation. So I'm the one that started Joe Oliver off from being a butler on third and magazine. He was the butler that when I got him. And I put him and we made up the Magnolia Band. And after we made up the Magnolia Band, Joe Oliver takes and we were figuring on getting uniforms. And Noah Dutrae was playing trambor. Sam Dutrae was playing clarinet. What's the name again? Little Happy was playing drum. I was playing guitar. Red Happy? Red Happy was playing drum. And I was playing guitar with him. And then they decided to put me manager of the band. And I signed all contracts. And Joe Oliver was taking the rung and we this and I told Nora. And all of us was together. And I turned around and I said well I'll take the manager but I wasn't particular about it. But I know it all about it anyhow. But I was you know. That works for an accident. So we decided to get uniforms from your serial rebutting company. Then after we cut up the money, we put up the money with Joe Oliver. Nora and all of the whole band put up the money. He was in, you know, the kid with the money. He was like the treasurer. He gets the money. Well he said so long with that money. And we never heard nothing about serial rebutting company with our uniforms. I want to find out and the rest of them want to find out what they're doing. Well Joe Oliver used to be uptown there on 2nd Street somewhere playing pool all the time. But we got nervous about that money. And I asked him many times, Joe when are you going to get out of the uniform? He said well I ain't got no answer yet. So we just fool around, fool around waiting, waiting, waiting. Until Joe hadn't spent our money. Joe hadn't spent our money. Joe hadn't spent the uniform. And he said well, I said well, Nora the reason why we thought you was with him, because you live uptown with him. And we thought that you was uptown with him. Well it happened that he fool around and he got the money some kind of way I don't know. But he sent boys and he got the uniforms. And that's the uniforms when I got there, yes. It was what I call a dark green with black stripes. And a dark green cap. And I got MGR on that cap. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. Manager. But we were thinking about throwing you over the money for what we had for a set, and we want our uniforms. And we want to know what he done that morning. Well, I had heard that he was playing pool, losing, and he had plenty of money in his pocket from the band. So we decided that we were going to take it and do something with it. Well, it happened that Joe come across, and he found about two weeks or three weeks after that, he got the money, and he appropriated. And he said, well, we got our uniforms, because we hadn't taken the measure and everything else. We had to get that. But after I started that, I'll take some turn around, and I said, well, Joe, I said, everything's all right now. I said, I'm glad you got the uniforms, no more trouble. So point thing, you know, we said, well, Joe, now, what are we going to lose the manager? He said, Lou is the manager of Norris. He said, Lou is the manager. All right. Well, all right. Lucian Pavilion. We played at different places, the White Owl. And in the, Sharky was, Sharky was out there playing. He was playing at the, at this whole, I love club, I believe, because we used to buck together, Sharky and I. And my brother also used to have the Olympia band. Well, he used to buck with Sharky. Well, he's all right, but he doesn't have much depth anymore.

Well, yeah, he's still a little small. He's pretty short, but he's got a stomach.

segments.title: Tape start and setting up the interview
segments.summary: Chatter about the tape and Freddie's first instruments, then Keppard agrees to tell about his life; he was born in 1888 in New Orleans.

segments.title: Brother Freddie Keppard and the first instruments
segments.summary: Keppard names his brother Freddie, one year younger, and says he himself started on guitar while Freddie began on violin with Mr. Baboy.

segments.title: Freddie's first jobs: Joe Petit, Hannan's Saloon, first cornet
segments.summary: Freddie played violin under Teton (Adolf Alexander) and with Joe Petit, got his first cornet from their father, and played his first cornet job at Lake Lucien Pavilion; Louis took over his job at the jewelry store.

segments.title: Freddie on mandolin and accordion; Manuel Manetta
segments.summary: Freddie played a little mandolin and the squeeze-box accordion but not in bands; Manuel Manetta is mentioned as a friend.

segments.title: What became of Freddie's cornet; Keppard's own lessons
segments.summary: Keppard holds Freddie's first little cornet; Herb Moran bought the later one from Freddie's wife. Keppard himself got cornet lessons from Mal Perez and Hippolyte Charles.

segments.title: Learning the value of time before an instrument; Bud Scott
segments.summary: Old teachers required learning time values before touching an instrument. Keppard left the store job and picked up guitar like Bud Scott, whom he praises.

segments.title: The Magnolia Band and Cherry Blossom Band members
segments.summary: Keppard lists the players in his Magnolia Band, then the Cherry Blossom Band, playing at Economy Hall and Copperhead Hall.

segments.title: Recruiting Joe Oliver and the uniform money trouble
segments.summary: Keppard says he got Joe Oliver out of butler work to join the Magnolia Band; as manager he chased Oliver, the treasurer, over missing uniform money until the green uniforms arrived. Band then played the lake spots.

segments.title: Sharkey Bonano, Freddie and Bunk, and the district joints
segments.summary: Keppard talks about Sharky's cornet, Freddie's fear of Bunk's Maple Leaf Rag, then playing in Storyville places on Custom House and Basin Streets.

segments.title: Quadrilles and dance repertoire; playing with Perez and Kid Punch
segments.summary: Keppard recalls card drills, mazurkas, lancers, and quadrilles at the halls and playing with Mal Perez and others.

segments.title: Brass band with Kid Punch, Black Benny and Zeb
segments.summary: Keppard played alto in his brass band with Black Benny, Henry Martin, Zeb and Kid Punch, whom he rates as having a stronger lift than Freddie.

segments.title: Frank Ducey's band and other old-timers
segments.summary: Keppard names sidemen who played with Frank Ducey and Jack Carey, and a still-active old timer, then returns to playing guitar after 1917.

segments.title: Lessons, Wooden Joe records, and Kid Howard
segments.summary: Keppard praises his teachers, mentions records with Wooden Joe Nicholas and playing at Graffanina's, and comments on Kid Howard and young players.

segments.title: The card drill dance and Little White's house musicians
segments.summary: Keppard describes the nine-part card drill in Economy Hall, then musicians at Little White's, including guitarist Stair Braddock.

segments.title: Hammonds, Hunter's and the Lindsays with Joe Oliver
segments.summary: Where Freddie played at Hannan's on Murray and Custom House; Keppard played across at Hunter's with Joe Oliver, Eddie Dorsey, and the Lindsays and Fosters.

segments.title: Franklin Street musicians and Tick Chambers; band photo question
segments.summary: Keppard names players on Franklin Street around Tick Chambers and the district closing; the tape ends with a question about a band photo with Roy Palmer.
